thread.title: Special Participation B: Qwen on HW10 Coding
thread.content: I used Qwen3-Max Thinking on the coding parts of Homework 10. I used a separate chat for each coding question, so there are 3 separate chat logs. Overall, Qwen had very strong performance and was almost able to one shot all of the questions, except for minor mistakes. It was able to understand everything very well, and one-shot all parts of question 2 all at once. Plugging the code into the full notebook, it was able to run without errors and give reasonable results. Question 3 log: https://chat.qwen.ai/c/25253f17-c753-45e4-b584-4fe65b874415Notes: Similar to question 2, I fed the template notebook as text, from the .py version. I also do want to note Qwen wasn’t able to completely one-shot this question, as it had some errors with assigning the GPU device – however, it’s logic was correct on the first shot. Thus it required a few more interactions with Qwen to have it arrive at the correct code. thread.document:
I used Qwen3-Max Thinking on the coding parts of Homework 10. I used a separate chat for each coding question, so there are 3 separate chat logs. Overall, Qwen had very strong performance and was almost able to one shot all of the questions, except for minor mistakes. 

Question 2 log: https://chat.qwen.ai/s/29ecf785-ec89-4e58-aab6-5f7675d8e02d?fev=0.0.248

Notes: Because Qwen is unable to accept ipynb or py files, I copied the text contents of the .py version, and gave it to Qwen as text input. It was able to understand everything very well, and one-shot all parts of question 2 all at once. Plugging the code into the full notebook, it was able to run without errors and give reasonable results. 

Question 3 log: https://chat.qwen.ai/c/25253f17-c753-45e4-b584-4fe65b874415

Notes: Similar to question 2, I fed the template notebook as text, from the .py version. In order to give the paper context on the Attention is All You Need paper that is cited in the question, I also uploaded it as a pdf. I also do want to note Qwen wasn’t able to completely one-shot this question, as it had some errors with assigning the GPU device – however, it’s logic was correct on the first shot. Thus it required a few more interactions with Qwen to have it arrive at the correct code. After plugging in the code it wrote into the original notebook and running it, here are the results:


Question 4 log: https://chat.qwen.ai/s/d3dde69f-6dda-4327-858e-cc4f3c6dda60?fev=0.0.248

Notes: I also fed the template notebook downloaded from the .py version. It was able to one-shot the code. I’m not sure if this was necessary – but I also uploaded the “BranchyNet: Fast Inference via Early Exiting from Deep Neural Networks” paper as a pdf to Qwen to provide it context on Early Exiting. It was able to fill in correct code and produce correct results. Here are results:
(i) Regular ResNet-18

Accuracy: ≈90.78% (0.9078333377838135)

Inference Speed: not explicitly measured; only tqdm progress is shown, no formal speed metric

Total MACS: 3,336,213,504,000

(ii) Early-exit ResNet-18 (entropy tolerance = 0.05 in notebook)

Accuracy: ≈90.78% (0.9078333377838135)

Inference Speed: not explicitly measured; tqdm progress suggests faster than baseline, but no formal metric

Total MACS: 2,305,700,339,712

(iii) How did early exit do? (compare)

Accuracy: Essentially unchanged (≈90.78% for both baseline and early exit).

MACS: Early exit uses about 1/1.4469 ≈ 69% of the baseline MACs, i.e. standard ResNet needs ~1.45× more MACs than early exit.

(iv) Lowest MACs found and what it says

Lowest MACs shown in the notebook outputs: 2,305,700,339,712 (for entropy tolerance 0.05).

Interpretation: Early exit can significantly cut compute (MACs) while keeping ≥90% accuracy, implying many inputs are “easy” and do not need the full depth.

(v) Early exit vs smaller model – when and why

Use early exit when:

Example difficulty varies a lot (many easy, some hard).

Use a smaller model when:

You want a single simple fixed‑cost model (no branches or thresholds).
